title: Barszcz biały
subtitle: Polish white borscht with sausage and egg
excerpt: A tangy, cream-enriched Polish soup made from fermented rye sour or soured wheat flour, with sliced kielbasa sausage and hard-boiled egg. Traditional Easter soup in Poland, served with horseradish.
sourceNotes: Barszcz biały (white borscht) is the Easter soup of Poland, distinct from red borscht. It is based on żur (fermented rye sour) and appears in virtually every Polish cookery reference. Cross-referenced with Zuza Zak, Polska (2016).

recipe.makeAheadNotes: The soup base can be made the day before. Add the eggs and sausage to order.

glossaryTerms.definition: A fermented sour made from rye flour and water, used as the base for barszcz biały and żurek soup in Poland. Gives a sharp, tangy flavour. Available bottled in Polish food shops; can be approximated with a mixture of soured cream and a little vinegar.

content.text: Barszcz biały gets its sourness from żur, a fermented rye liquid that gives the soup a distinctive tangy depth. Bottled żur is available in Polish food shops; it will say 'zakwas żytni' or 'żur' on the label. If you cannot find it, use 200 ml of soured cream thinned with a little lemon juice and cider vinegar as a shortcut, though the flavour is different.

items.prepNote: for thickening, mixed to a paste with 50 ml cold water
or to taste, for sourness in place of żur
kielbasa or smoked sausage, sliced 1 cm thick

content.text: Bring the stock to a simmer with the bay leaves, allspice, garlic, and marjoram. Simmer for 10 minutes. Remove the whole spices.
Add the sliced sausage and simmer for 5 minutes. If using diced potato, add it and cook until tender.

In a bowl, whisk the soured cream with the flour paste until smooth. Ladle a cup of the hot soup into the soured cream mixture and whisk to combine (tempering it to prevent curdling). Pour the mixture back into the soup, stirring constantly.
Add the cider vinegar and stir. Heat gently until the soup thickens slightly; do not boil. Taste and adjust sourness, salt, and pepper.
Place 2 halves of hard-boiled egg in each bowl and ladle the hot soup and sausage over. Serve with horseradish alongside.

items.symptom: The soured cream curdled in the soup
items.cause: Not tempered before adding, or soup was too hot
items.fix: Always temper: ladle hot soup into the soured cream, whisk, then add to the pot. Do not boil after adding cream.

items.symptom: The soup is not sour enough
items.fix: Add more cider vinegar a teaspoon at a time. The sourness is the defining character of this soup.

items.cause: Not enough flour in the thickener
items.fix: Make a separate slurry of 1 tbsp flour and 2 tbsp cold water, whisk into the hot soup, and simmer for 5 minutes.

items.cause: Dried marjoram is more pungent than fresh
items.fix: Reduce to 1/2 tsp. Marjoram is essential but should be a background note, not the main flavour.

content.text: Barszcz biały is the Easter soup of Poland. It is served on Easter Sunday morning (Wielkanoc) as part of a tradition called Śniadanie Wielkanocne, or Easter breakfast, after the blessing of food at church the previous day. The white borscht is eaten alongside ham, sausage, coloured eggs, and a sweet bread called babka. The sour, warming soup breaks the Lenten fast. It is also eaten throughout winter at home.
